passages.t: The Levites ask for their towns
passages.happening:
The heads of the families of Levi come to Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the leaders of the tribes at Shiloh. They make a claim: “The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities in which to live, together with pasturelands for our livestock” (verse 2).

“So by the command of the LORD, the Israelites gave the Levites these cities and their pasturelands out of their own inheritance” (verse 3).

The towns are assigned by lot to the four groups of Levites. The priests, the descendants of Aaron, receive thirteen towns from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin. The rest of the Kohathites receive ten, from Ephraim, Dan and half of Manasseh. The Gershonites receive thirteen in the north. The Merarites receive twelve, from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun (verses 4-7).
passages.hearers:
The Levites were the tribe set apart for the service of God. The priests among them, Aaron's line, offered the sacrifices. The other Levites looked after the tent of God's presence and all that belonged to it. Moses had also said that they were to teach Israel God's law.

They had been given no region of their own. But they had to live somewhere, and Moses had commanded that each tribe give them towns. Like the daughters of Zelophehad, the Levites come and say what God commanded, and it is done.

The words ‘out of their own inheritance’ matter. The towns were not spare land. Every tribe gave up some of what it had just received. The first thing Israel does with its new inheritance is to give part of it away for the service of God.

Pasturelands were the open ground around a town's walls, where animals could graze. The Levites lived in the towns and kept flocks on this common land. They did not own the farmland beyond. For their living they depended on the tithes and offerings of the people.

The priests' towns all lay in the south, among Judah, Simeon and Benjamin. That is the part of the country where the temple would one day be built. The text does not say whether this was planned or simply how the lot fell.
passages.later:
The command was given on the plains of Moab: “Command the Israelites to give, from the inheritance they will possess, cities for the Levites to live in and pasturelands around the cities” (Numbers 35:2).

Moses said what the tribe was for: “He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel; he will set incense before You and whole burnt offerings on Your altar” (Deuteronomy 33:10).
passages.asks: Each tribe gave towns ‘out of their own inheritance’ so that God's servants could live among them. Ask what you set aside, out of what you have been given, for the worship of God and the teaching of his word. Ask whether the people who serve and teach in your church are provided for, and whether you have ever thought of that as your business.

passages.happening:
The writer lists the towns by name, group by group, and after nearly every group he adds that they came ‘together with their pasturelands’.

The priests receive Hebron in the hill country of Judah, though its fields and villages remain Caleb's (verses 11-12). Their other towns include Libnah, Debir and Beth-shemesh, and in Benjamin, Gibeon and Anathoth (verses 13-18). The other Kohathites receive Shechem and Gezer among their towns (verses 20-26). The Gershonites receive Golan in Bashan and Kedesh in Galilee (verses 27-33). The Merarites receive Bezer and Ramoth in Gilead among theirs (verses 34-40).

“For the Levites, then, there were forty-eight cities in all, together with their pasturelands, within the territory of the Israelites” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
Look at where the towns are. They are in every tribe, north and south, east and west of the Jordan. No Israelite village was very far from a town where Levites lived.

That spread had a purpose. The Levites were the keepers and teachers of God's law. If they had all lived around the sanctuary, most of Israel would rarely have seen them. Scattered through forty-eight towns, they lived among the people they were meant to teach.

There is an old sorrow turned to good here. Jacob had said on his deathbed that Levi's descendants would be scattered in Israel, because of Levi's violence. They are scattered. But the scattering has become a gift to every tribe.

All six cities of refuge are in the list: Hebron, Shechem, Kedesh, Golan, Bezer and Ramoth. A person running for his life would arrive in a town full of people whose calling was to know the law and to judge by it.

Some familiar names appear. Gibeon, the town that tricked Israel in chapter 9, becomes a town of priests. Anathoth would later be the home of the prophet Jeremiah, who came from a priestly family.

Even Caleb gives something. Hebron was his, won at eighty-five. The town itself goes to the priests, and Caleb keeps the fields and villages around it.

A similar list of these towns appears in the first book of Chronicles, with some differences in the names. Lists like this were copied and brought up to date over time, and scholars differ about when this one took its form.
passages.later:
Jacob's words over Levi were, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7).

Peter writes to Christians scattered through many lands and gives them the Levites' calling: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9).
passages.asks: The Levites were scattered so that no village would be far from someone who knew God's word. Ask where you have been ‘scattered’: the street, the office, the school or the family where you are the one who knows it. Ask whether you think of that place as an accident or as an assignment. And ask what old sorrow in your family's story God might be turning to good.

passages.t: ‘Not one of all the LORD’s good promises’
passages.happening:
The lists stop, and the writer steps back to say what it has all meant.

“Thus the LORD gave Israel all the land He had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it” (verse 43).

“And the LORD gave them rest on every side, just as He had sworn to their fathers. None of their enemies could stand against them, for the LORD delivered all their enemies into their hand” (verse 44).

“Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled” (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
These three verses are the summit of the book. Everything from the first chapter has been climbing toward them.

They answer the first chapter almost word for word. There God said he was giving the land, that no one would be able to stand against Joshua, and that he would give the people rest. Here the writer says: he gave the land, no enemy stood, he gave rest.

The promises reach back further than Joshua. ‘He had sworn to give their fathers’ means Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. God had told Abraham, a childless man living in a tent, that his descendants would have this land. Centuries had passed. Abraham's family had been slaves in Egypt and wanderers in a desert. The writer looks at farms, towns and borders and says that God did what he said.

The subject of every main verb is the LORD. He gave. He gave rest. He delivered. Israel ‘took possession’ and ‘settled’, but only of what was given.

The word ‘all’ rings through the verses: all the land, on every side, all their enemies, not one promise. A reader who remembers chapter 13, with its long list of land not yet taken, will feel the strain. The hard question below takes it up.

For now it is enough to hear what the writer most wants heard. Before the book turns to warnings, and it is about to, it wants one thing fixed in the reader's mind. God can be trusted. Whatever goes wrong later in Israel's story will not be because God failed to keep his word.
passages.later:
Joshua says it again in his farewell, as a man about to die: ‘not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed’ (Joshua 23:14). King Solomon said it at the opening of the temple: “Not one word has failed of all the good promises He made through His servant Moses” (1 Kings 8:56).

The letter to the Hebrews honors this rest and says there is more: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day. There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8-9).

Paul says where all God's promises meet: “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
passages.hard:
How can the book say that God gave Israel all the land, when it has just said that much of the land was not taken?

The strain is real, and the book puts it in plain sight. Chapter 13 says that very much of the land remained. Chapters 15 to 17 name cities the tribes could not take. And these verses say that the LORD gave all the land he had sworn to give.

Readers have answered in three ways.

Many hold that the summary speaks of what God had done. He had given the land and broken the power of its kings. The earlier notes describe what Israel had not yet taken hold of. On this view the gift was complete where Israel's possession of it was not.

Others note that summaries in the ancient world used sweeping language as a matter of course, and that no first reader would have taken these verses to deny what the same book reports a few pages earlier.

Some scholars think the book sets side by side sources with different emphases.

These notes do not choose. All of these readers agree that the writer wants God's faithfulness heard first. The chapters that follow, and the book of Judges, then make it clear that Israel's enjoyment of the gift depended on Israel's own faithfulness.

These verses speak of God's promise to ancient Israel as this book tells it. They are not a statement about any border, state or claim to land today.
passages.asks: The writer stopped and said it plainly: not one promise failed. Ask whether you could say that about your own life with God so far, and what you would have to remember in order to say it. Ask which promise of God you find hardest to believe today. And ask whether you are living as someone who has been given rest, or as someone still trying to earn it.
